doc.title: Mark Soskin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 17, 2021

title: A Jimmy Ponder record date and The Creator Has a Master Plan
summary: Soskin describes how the Ponder call came, the band, and how he approached the long vamp on The Creator Has a Master Plan with voicings and minor scales.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Can you describe to me if I looked, I’m looking at your sideman list right now and I’ll pick okay Jimmy Ponder.
So you get a call — tell me how that whole thing works.

Okay so I got a call from — who did I get it from — well I got a call from he was the bass player I think on that record, or something like that. And he said, “Yeah I’ve got this record date coming up and it’s for Jimmy Ponder, you want to do it?” I said, “Yeah, sure

I’d love to do it. I know Jimmy Ponder’s music.” And so then what I did, I started checking out Jimmy’s music and trying to see what I could do with it. I remember we did, on that record date, “The Creator Has a Master Plan.” And you know that’s really not a typical tune you would do. But you know I knew about it enough where I could do something with it. And that was great. I believe the bass player on that record was Peter Washington I think. And oh, and the drummer was the guy who played on “Song for my Father.” The drummer from that record.
Oh I should know this. I’m not passing the audition at the moment.
But anyway it was that drummer. So it was a nice band.
I just heard that recording by the way on my, whatever delivery system I have, Pandora or something. And I heard his version of that. So I was just listening to you a couple of days ago.

And when you have a tune like that, that’s long, lengthy vamps, and the harmonic material is let’s say limited, how do you expand on that without — you have to keep the music in mind and respect the composition.
So how do you build on those two vamping chords?

Yeah well you know I think it was in C minor and you know with the voicings you know you’d play certain voicings when it came to it, maybe fourth voicing. And then for soloing you know C minor, all the minor chords you’d use, the scales you know, all of that. And that has to do with improvising. You know that’s pretty much what I’m going to do today when I teach this class is what scales go with the chords. And you have to know those chords. You have to know those scales. So I’ve done that work.
